introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 3 (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic maps, Graph Paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: 7 a) Examine the distribution of water resources in Cameroon. **(7 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Cameroon is relatively well endowed with water, but the resources are **unevenly distributed in space and time**: abundant in the south and west, scarce in the north.

**Rainfall (the source of all other resources).** Annual rainfall is **very high on the coast and on Mt Cameroon** (several thousand millimetres), heavy in the south and in the western highlands (about 1,500 to 2,500 mm), and decreases northwards to the Adamawa and the Benue, and to the Sahel of the Far North, where it is often below about 600 mm and unreliable.

**Surface water.**

- **Rivers:** four main drainage basins. The **Atlantic basin** (Sanaga, Wouri, Nyong, Ntem and Mungo) is the most important; the **Congo basin** in the east (Sangha, Dja and Ngoko) drains the forested south-east; the **Niger basin** in the north and west (the Benue and its tributaries, such as the Faro, Mayo Kebbi and Katsina Ala) and the **Lake Chad basin** (Logone and Chari) in the far north.
- **Lakes:** natural lakes such as **Lake Chad** (shared with its neighbours and shrinking), crater lakes (Nyos, Barombi Mbo, Oku) and artificial lakes behind dams: **Lagdo** on the Benue, **Mbakaou, Bamendjin**, **Lom Pangar** and **Maga**.
- **Wetlands, swamps and mangroves** on the coast and floodplains of the Logone.

**Groundwater.** Aquifers in the **sedimentary basins** (Douala, Lake Chad) and in the weathered or fractured basement rock and volcanic areas; they are especially important for **water supply in the north and in rural areas** through wells and boreholes. There are also **mineral springs** in the western highlands and Mt Cameroon.

**Conclusion.** There is thus a clear **north-south contrast**: a surplus in the south, west and the coast, and a deficit in the far north where water must be stored in dams and lakes and drawn from boreholes.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) (i) Locate and describe the spatial pattern of rail way transport network in Cameroon. **(8 marks)**

(ii) Account for its present declining state. **(8 marks)**

**(Total = 23 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
### (i) Location and pattern of the railway network (8 marks)

Cameroon has a **small, narrow-gauge (1 metre), mostly single-track** railway of roughly one thousand kilometres operated today by a concession company (**Camrail**). It consists of:

1. **The Central (Trans-Cameroon) line**, running **Douala - Yaounde - Ngaoundere**: it leaves the port of Douala, crosses Edea and Eseka, reaches **Yaounde** (the capital) and goes on north-eastwards through the Centre and East of the country to **Ngaoundere** on the Adamawa Plateau, where the railhead is the transfer point to road transport for the north and for Chad and the Central African Republic. Together this is the longest line, with the Yaounde-Ngaoundere section about 600 km long (built in the 1970s).
2. **The Western (Mungo) line**, from Douala north-westwards via **Mbanga** to **Nkongsamba**, serving the banana and coffee area of Moungo (about 170 km).
3. **Branch lines**, such as the Mbanga - Kumba spur in the South-West and the Yaounde - Mbalmayo spur.

**Pattern.** The network is **linear and branching (dendritic)** and **converges on Douala**, the main port; it runs from the coast inland along **two axes** (north-east and north-west); and it **does not form a loop**. Large areas are not served: the **Far North, the extreme East, the South-East and most of the North-West and the South** (Kribi). There is **no link with the networks of neighbouring countries**. The lines mainly carry **goods** (timber, petroleum products, cement, agricultural produce and imports) and passengers between the main cities.

### (ii) Causes of the decline of the railway (8 marks)

1. **Competition from road transport:** roads are more flexible, door-to-door, and cheaper for short and medium trips; many minibuses and buses (and the tarred Douala - Yaounde road) have taken passengers and goods.
2. **Old and insufficient infrastructure and rolling stock:** the 1-metre gauge, single track, sharp curves and old coaches and wagons limit speed and capacity; delays and breakdowns reduce reliability. Heavy maintenance has been neglected.
3. **Accidents and a loss of confidence:** accidents such as the Eseka derailment in 2016 raised safety concerns and reduced demand.
4. **Lack of investment and financial difficulties:** the high cost of renewing track and equipment and of operating loss-making branches means that passenger services on some lines (Mungo, Kumba) were reduced or suspended.
5. **Decline in the traffic served:** a fall in agricultural exports on some branches, and the closure or decline of some agro-industries and mines, reduced freight; flooding and landslides sometimes cut the track.
6. **Poor management and institutional problems**, and the **limited coverage**, which means that the railway cannot connect all production areas to markets.
7. **Insecurity in some areas** (for example the North-West and South-West since 2017) has also disturbed activity.

**Conclusion.** The decline results from road competition, ageing equipment, under-investment and a limited, poorly integrated network. Modernisation of the track, rolling stock and management would be required to restore its role.
